changes.before:
The bill covers bargaining for a first contract after a union is newly recognized or certified. If there is no agreement 90 days after bargaining starts, either side may ask for mediation from the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service (FMCS), the U.S. agency that provides mediators: “either party may notify the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service that a dispute exists, and may request mediation.” [1] A mediator cannot decide the dispute. If there is still no agreement 30 days after that request, the dispute goes to arbitration, where a panel decides: “the Service shall refer the dispute to a 3-person arbitration panel” [1].

The panel has “one member selected by the individual or labor organization, one member selected by the employer, and one neutral member mutually agreed to by the parties.” [1] If a side does not choose its member, “the Service shall designate any members not selected by the individual or labor organization or by the employer.” [1] The panel majority’s decision binds both sides for two years unless both agree in writing to change it. Either waiting period can be longer only if both sides agree.

Under the law in force on June 9, 2026, there is no such route. The duty to bargain “does not compel either party to agree to a proposal or require the making of a concession” [2].

The panel route applies only to a first contract, not to later contracts. The bill sets no deadline for the panel’s decision: “it does not limit the timeline of arbitration.” [3]

Under current law, neither side has to agree to anything. Under the bill, either side can start the route to a panel after the waiting periods, and neither side can stop the panel by refusing to choose its member. More time needs both sides’ agreement.

changes.before:
Under existing law, upon reaching a good-faith impasse, “the NLRA entitles an employer to unilaterally implement its last, best, and final offer.” [1] The NLRA is the main U.S. private-sector labor law. The bill adds a duty “to maintain current wages, hours, and terms and conditions of employment pending an agreement” [2].

Labor lawyer Robert Steptoe reads this duty as one that “extends indefinitely beyond the point when the parties reach a good faith impasse to the date the parties reach agreement.” [3] He adds that it “applies not just to first contracts, but rather to all employers and all contracts.” [3]

This reading comes from law-firm analyses, not a court ruling. The duty keeps both good and bad current terms, so it can stop an employer from either cutting them or raising them on its own. The sources give no figure for how often employers make such changes today.

Each of these kinds of term is assessed separately after this claim.

changes.before: Time for worship. changes.after: This bill would change U.S. labor law for workers who have newly formed a union. An employer would have to begin talks soon after the union asks. If the two sides cannot agree on a first contract, either side can ask a federal agency for mediation. If mediation does not produce an agreement, a three-person panel decides, and both sides must follow the panel’s decision for two years. The bill would also require current pay and working conditions to stay in place during talks and would keep an employer’s duty to bargain until workers remove the union in an election.
